utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, technical booth, the interpreters. Good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley. Good morning, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic. Good morning, General Krstic. Good morning, Witness. Are you feeling rested today? Fine. As you know, today you're going to answer questions which Mr. Petrusic is going to put to you. I would like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution. Good morning, Witness V. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, did you acquire your initial skills in radio telegraphy in the army of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I'm not a telegraphist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your initial knowledge about electronic surveillance and radio interception acquired in the army of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. I was a signalman in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you deployed in the unit for electronic surveillance and radio interception in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, I have no intention of showing you a statement that you gave to the Prosecution, but can you remember saying, on the 6th and 12th of May, 1999, when you were interviewed, that you were engaged in those activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a signalman in the JNA, and I engaged in these activities only in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your training last regarding communication systems in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the vocational training in communications -- did that take place throughout those six months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first three months were devoted to general training, and the second three months to more specialist training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you engaged in electronic reconnaissance and radio interception?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at (redacted), which devices did you use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were amateur radio devices which were refurbished to be adjusted to the needs we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there was any difference between the equipment and the devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was there any difference between the equipment that you used and devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a difference. As I have already told you, those were amateur devices that were adjusted to our needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to monitor a conversation, what was essential in terms of equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd rather not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a military secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us call it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific without saying -- without the qualification of uncertainty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the army you belonged to supplied photographs of that equipment, Exhibit 298 and 299, does that mean that you are still under the obligation to keep this as a military secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your will?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could interrupt Mr. Petrusic, and could I ask for a closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, do you agree we're going to go into closed session or, rather, private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can explain myself once we're in closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Closed session, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: redacted) redacted) redacted) redacted) redacted) redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were monitoring a "conversation," let me put that in quotation marks, you took it down on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the conversations. If there was a shortage of notebooks, then this would be taken down on pieces of paper which would later be bound together. But most of those were lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those that were not lost, what did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over to the superior command ad acta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they forwarded by means of a computer that was installed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Written reports were sent by computer and the notebooks that were filled in completely would be forwarded by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, I should like to use an example and ask you, as a specialist in the area, to explain it for us. If, by way of example, Zlatar calls Badem -- you know the code names, the secret names -- or to be more practical, if Bratunac calls Vlasenica, do you hear both participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends. Sometimes it is possible to hear both; sometimes one; sometimes one is more audible than the other. It depends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular example, can you tell us what that depends on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the direction of the antenna and the locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two participants in the conversation, were they on the same frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, fully appreciating Mr. Cayley's objection, I would propose we go back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see in the public gallery that we are in public session, so you may continue, Mr. Petrusic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, Exhibit 283 of the Prosecution, please look at the highlighted page 30 with the initials in the upper right-hand corner, "W.E." Witness V, you can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just out of caution, there is actually a signature on that page of somebody that could be identified potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, you're right. Perhaps we could cover or hide the signature with a piece of paper. Before putting it on the ELMO, conceal the signature with a sticker, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as the number and the initials are the subject of my question, perhaps it would be better not to place it on the ELMO but just to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, unfortunately it was placed on the ELMO, so maybe if we could -- if you could make an order essentially to stop the public feed on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar, we need to redact the showing of this document, so the signature needs to be redacted, perhaps the whole document that was shown on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the booth is indicating to me that they didn't switch to public feed, so it never went out on the television screen. So the problem doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I think it is possible to show the exhibit with this small sticker on it, or focus on number 30 and the initials "W.E." Mr. Usher, are you following me? Show only this part here. Yes. I think it is the upper corner, the upper right-hand corner. Fine. Mr. Petrusic, I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I knew this would have caused so many problems, I could have withdrawn that question, but anyway ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, this page that carries the number 30 and the initials below, were they placed there by you or one of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't note that down. Perhaps one of my colleagues did. Actually, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether one of your colleagues had a similar signature to this and these initials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions. Witness V, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I only have really one question for you. Mr. Petrusic asked you in your cross-examination, when you were listening to a transmission, whether you could hear both parties to the conversation. And your answer was that sometimes you could hear both parties and sometimes you could only hear one party, and it depended on a number of factors. The question that I have for you is simply this: Isn't it a fact that it was possible to monitor both participants in a conversation, and in fact you did on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many occasions, you could follow both participants, as I've already said. There were situations where one participant was not very audible, not as audible as the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when one of the parties was not audible, what did you write down in your written note of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, if we couldn't hear at all, then we would make a note of it and say that one of the participants was completely inaudible. If it was partially audible, then we would put three dots where it was not audible and continue with the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions for the witness. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions? No. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness V, I just have a few general questions. The first is: Based on your knowledge and experience in both the JNA army and later in the Bosnian army, is it generally true that when parties are speaking, military parties, to one another on these lines, they have a general notion that they may be intercepted? I mean are they aware that there may be interceptions by a different -- by an opposition force? I mean generally aware. I'm not asking you about any specific situation, but are they not generally aware that these relay stations are in existence and may be monitoring them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to some army rules, this should be respected. That is to say, they ought to know that they might be monitored. In most cases, depending on the circumstances and in wartime, they don't always adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So they have a general idea that there's a good chance they might be monitored. I think you've answered that, so I'll go on to the second question. Are there, without again getting specific in any way, are there ways in which, say, two military posts in the same army could communicate with each other by radio that would not -- that couldn't be intercepted, that would defy being intercepted? I mean do they have defensive devices so that they won't be intercepted, or encryption, or something so that the opposite force would not be able to intercept them? I don't want to know what they are, but do those -- if they really need to convey some secret material from Post A to Post B, are there ways? I don't want to know what they are, but are there ways that they can do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course that exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So my third question then is: If somebody in Post A wanted to convey something that was very sensitive or delicate to Post B, why would they use an open -- or a line in which there was a risk, a real risk, of interception? Why would they not use whatever these devices are that would be much harder or impossible to intercept? I mean, are there reasons, based on your observations and knowledge in both armies, that would explain why somebody who had some very sensitive information would use a line that was very possibly open to interception?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, number one, perhaps they don't have any other means of communication. Secondly, usually people think, "Well, they won't hear me this time." So those are the two sort of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness V, I have two questions for you. You said that one of the factors which could facilitate communication was the direction of the antennae. As you know, the communication channels here are wavelengths, airwaves. How do climatic conditions or how can the climate and climatic conditions influence communications? Or to put it another way, can the climate influence communication lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain that to us a little?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert in that field, I'm afraid, so I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, in January or July, in principle, what is a better time, a better season for communicating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably July, at least in the cases I worked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, is it July or January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] July. Thank you. Another question. We saw the numbering of the pages with the initials, the "WV" and the "E." When you wrote your notes -- you did the transcript of this little notebook -- were those page numbers already there or were the pages numbered once the notebook had been completed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received our notebooks, the pages were already numbered, because this was a measure of precaution, to avoid somebody ripping out the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Witness V, good morning. Just to follow up on the question asked by my colleague. You were in the JNA for some time. Did you receive any kind of directions or instructions that when there is something very sensitive you should not transmit it through any means which could be intercepted? Were there some kinds of things which should not be done in this way which could be intercepted? You said there were other means. Were there military rules for protection of very secretive information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. You had to use certain codes and so on, names, so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This would be sufficient protection, or were there other means of keeping items which cannot be reached in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: My work post, the work I did, we had to adhere to some of these things. But in other jobs, on other posts, the protective measures might have been more stringent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you think that there were other means which cannot be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness V. That brings you to the end of your testimony here at the Tribunal. We should like to thank you for coming and wish you bon voyage to your country. Do not get out of your seat straight away because you enjoy protective measures. I think we need to take a break to prepare for the next witness. Mr. Cayley, I think we also have exhibits to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What you just mentioned, Mr. President, in respect of a break, we've spoken with our learned colleagues, a 15-minute break because the next witness requires voice distortion and that has to be set up, so now would be an appropriate time. If I may deal with the exhibits before that. There are two photographs, Exhibits 298 and 299. Then there are seven intercepts. Bearing in mind the decision of the Court yesterday, Your Honours, in which you were delaying admission of the notebooks, I merely wish to raise a small point. I'm in no way wishing to challenge a decision that's already been made, but in respect of the individual intercepts, these are very short, brief extracts. My understanding of the rationale behind your general decision was the fact that the Defence were being expected to agree to admission of a very large document which they had not had the opportunity to read in its entirety. I don't believe that that would prevent from being admitted the individual intercepts, because they are, as I say, one-and-a-half-page extracts. They can be read. The witness has offered foundation for them. So I would offer into evidence Exhibits 313A, B, and C, 314A, B, and C, 315A, B, and C, 316A, B, and C, 317A, B, and C, 318A and B, and 318/1A and B. And -- sorry, my colleague has just informed me -- 316/1A, B, and C. That is, of course, on the understanding that the notebooks themselves, from which these documents are extracted and translated, are not yet admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, are you able at this point to state your views with regard to yesterday's exhibits and the ones tendered today? Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with respect to these two exhibits, 298 and 299, the Defence has no objections to make there in view of what Mr. Cayley has just presented. But these transcripts of the radio communications are, once again, a source from this overall material that we have received. I do not wish at any point, in any way, to be taken as justification on the part of the Defence counsel, but the Defence is still not able to say whether it agrees to the exhibits or objects to them. We are still not able to say, so my position is the same as it was during yesterday's proceedings, and at the end of this session, I would like to reserve the right to either agree to the documents tendered or to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Simply this, Mr. President, and I don't wish to sort of repeat myself ad nauseam: My understanding of the Court's decision was that additional time was to be given to the Defence because they had not had sufficient time to read all of these three volumes in their entirety. These are very short documents, the extracts; they can be read very quickly. The witness has provided foundation by identifying his handwriting and confirming that he took them down. By admitting these into evidence, it in no way admits the entire notebook, so the linkage for the Prosecution in that respect is still missing. But, as I say, the witness has identified these, he's provided foundation, and it's my view, my submission, that they should be admitted into evidence at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, let me just make sure I understand your position. Suppose we were to admit these excerpts into evidence now, and then in a week or so or whenever, Defence counsel, they had some objection to the accuracy or something of the notebook translation as it was later typed up into the written report, to the report which has been admitted. In your view, would they be able to make that objection now that the report itself had already been admitted? I think that's the only concern that we would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what was actually going through my mind was this: It was actually economy in use of witness. I'm sorry I may not actually be answering your question directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We had a single witness who identified all of these books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the Defence raise a problem with all of the books in their entirety, we would call that one witness back. Each of these individual intercepts extracted from the notebooks have been identified by a particular witness. If these are admitted now -- and I have to say for the moment, and I can't speak for the Defence, I can't see what objection they can make to this specific document because they've been able to read it and it it's very brief -- we would not then have to call back each of the intercept operators to answer questions on each of the individual exhibits. I know it's not Mr. Petrusic's intention that we should call back all of these witnesses, but we may find ourselves in a position where we would have to do so. So that's where my thought in this was coming from. I don't believe it places the Defence at a disadvantage because the source, the books which we need to rely on to make the evidential link, are still not admitted into evidence yet. That's a piece of our puzzle that we still have to get in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. So suppose, worst-case scenario, something happens and the books don't get admitted into evidence, would that automatically invalidate these transcripts if they had already been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour, based on the Rules of Evidence with which I've become familiar. Perhaps our systems -- perhaps the answer to your question would be, "Yes," but I think here it would perhaps lower their value on the scale of evidence. But I do believe that you would still be able to consider them in evidence. You just wouldn't have the source book available. It would perhaps be a "7" rather than a "10", to put it crudely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the documents and their admittance, the Chamber feels that they should be taken together. It is true that they are of a different nature, but we're going to give them the same treatment all together and we are going to give the Defence time to pronounce themselves. But I should like to tell the Defence that it is important, with respect to the Prosecutor's job, to know whether the documents are admitted or not. So as soon as the Defence counsel can give us a response -- it would be advisable by the end of the week -- please do so, and don't leave it to the last moment. It is true that the Chamber has made a decision, but the Chamber also understands that it is very important for the Prosecution to know whether they can count on those documents or not. And it is in that light that we are going to accord the same conditions to these documents, except 298 and 299, which have been admitted today. But with respect to the other documents, we would be following the same regime but would like to ask the Defence counsel to give us a timely response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry. There's four more exhibits which I suspect my learned colleagues will not have a problem with. 138 and 139, which were maps offered by my learned friend Mr. Harmon, the first map showing the operator locations at (redacted), 139 showing lines of radio communication. 137 was the list of call signs legend, and 300 was the list of operators which the previous witness identified. That document should be under seal because it identifies many of the witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Cayley -- yes, very well. I have just received the interpretation, so that's all right. So that particular one was under seal. Mr. Petrusic, with respect to the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no objections to make to the documents put forward, but I feel that Document 137, Lasta, that it should read " Istra" and not "Lasta". But that is just a suggestion on my part. That is to say, we suggest that the Prosecution check that word out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have no other objections to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, do you accept the suggestion made to you by the Defence, to replace "Lasta" by " Istra"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I think rather than myself giving an answer, we should actually check with the witnesses with whom we're dealing, because I'm not an expert on this. It's possible that we made a mistake in the name of the call sign. But my understanding also is that these call signs did change from time to time, so I would appreciate that possibility and maybe we will amend it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So 137, Exhibit 137, was shown to the witness as it stands. Mr. Petrusic, all these exhibits, 138, 137, 139, are public ones, and the other one is under seal. If there are any corrections, we can introduce them later on. But otherwise, they are admitted. 300 is under seal. We will now have a 20-minute recess to prepare the courtroom for the next witness. Witness V, please remain seated for a few more minutes. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps you could get closer to the microphone, please. Move closer to the microphone, please. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are now going to see your name written on the piece of paper that the usher is going to show you, and tell us, yes or no, whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Harmon, who is on your right, please. Show it to the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues for the Defence. Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to be referring to you as "Witness W" throughout the course of your testimony. Now, Witness W, can you tell me, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what country do you come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I come from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Judges your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. I have a two-year post-secondary education as a teacher of technical education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently employed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I'm working in AID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does "AID" stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It stands for the Agency for Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation that I heard was "Agency for Investigation and Documentation". Is that a correct description or is it the Agency for Information and Documentation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You received the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the agency for which you worked, AID, was it named the Service for State Security or SDB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been employed by SDB since 1982?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Correct. From 1982, I worked there continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'd like to turn your attention now to the time period when there was war in Bosnia, specifically in December of 1994, and ask you at that time did you form an electronic surveillance unit composed of members from the SDB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: A minor correction. I didn't form it, but the service in those days had a job classification which envisaged a department of which at the time I was the head. It is correct that in December, such a department had already been formed by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of this particular unit you've just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The purpose. I wouldn't call it a unit. It wasn't a military unit. It was a department of the service. And its purpose was to go on site, to choose an appropriate location, and to survey and intercept radio waves and thereby acquire interesting information for the needs of our service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and other members of your service conduct those activities from December of 1994 until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It is true that we engaged in those activities in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have the assistance of the usher, please, and if I could have the usher place Prosecutor's Exhibit 138 on the ELMO. 138 is a map. Mr. Usher, that's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, can you tell the Judges where you conducted these activities from, from what location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: In the period from 1994 until the end of 1995, I was at the location at (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the witness has pointed to that location on Prosecutor's Exhibit 138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, how many men were working with you in this particular endeavour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how you conducted your work in terms of shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Our work was conducted in shifts. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Q.Now, you've informed us that your unit was working at the location of (redacted), and my question is: Did the army also have an Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit at that same location conducting similar activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, this was an army facility in which we used only one room. It is a facility in which our corps had its own sections for reconnaissance, and we were given this one room to use which we did use. So we engaged in the same activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, while you engaged in the same activities, was your work separate and independent from the similar work being conducted by the army units at that same location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The work was separate but it was not completely independent because we coordinated in many areas. Should I explain that further?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Witness W. When I say "independent," you didn't use the same staff members that the army used in attempting to intercept communications, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That is correct. We had civilians and they had soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, you touched on it in your previous answer, your physical location where you were conducting your intercept operations was in a different part of the facility than where the army was conducting its intercept operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It was the same facility. I wouldn't like to describe it, but within that one building, we were one of the rooms in a row, the room that was free, unoccupied, at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness W, my point is that you were in a separate room with members of your unit conducting your activities; the army, at the same facility, was conducting its activities from different rooms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That is correct. We had that one room in which we worked, stayed, and even slept in our free time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In spite of the differences between the two units, the army unit and the unit from the SDB, did you use similar types of equipment to attempt to capture enemy radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, very similar equipment. The equipment had the same system of work. One could distinguish the model or the type, the manufacturer of the equipment. It had a different manufacturer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'm not a radio aficionado, but you have become quite familiar with the techniques that were used to intercept these enemy communications. Were the techniques employed by the SDB unit and the techniques that were employed by the army units at (redacted) similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness W, could you enlighten us, please, as to the different objectives between the types of communications in general that your unit was attempting to intercept and, to the extent that you know it, the types of communication the army was attempting to intercept? The reason I ask you that question is I'd like you to shed some light on why two units at the same location, using similar equipment and techniques, were operating. Could you shed some light on this issue for us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: In that period, that is, at that time in December 1994, when we moved into that location, our main aim was to collect information regarding the interests of the State Security Service. I don't know whether it is necessary for me to explain what kind of information those are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, suffice it to say it wasn't exclusively military information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We did not collect military information, but if, in the course of our activities, we came by such information, we would pass it on to the army unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is perfectly clear, in July of 1995 when the VRS took over the enclave of Srebrenica, was your unit operating from (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of time when the enclave fell, did your unit collect military communications and record military communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. In that period we did not -- we were not particular. The situation was such that we all had to dedicate all our efforts to everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me talk about the cooperation and the coordination between your intercept unit and the army units that were also intercepting communications. Did the army share with you intercepted communications that it received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Let me elaborate a little. It was not customary until then to exchange information at that level of that type, but when this situation became so difficult, we did so on the spot. We agreed and implemented the agreement and exchanged information throughout in both directions; that is, the army would share their information with us and we would share all our information with them, at (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "at this period of time," are you referring to the period of time when the enclave of Srebrenica fell to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and throughout the time of the events that followed after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you exchange this information, at a minimum, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, we exchanged them on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you exchange the information more often if the information that the army had intercepted was very urgent, very important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the urgency. We would assess the urgency in such a way that we classified information as especially urgent and ordinary information. We didn't make any further distinctions in assessing urgency. It was either very urgent or not very urgent. Very urgent information was exchanged immediately, and just the urgent, several times during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'd like you to explain mechanically how the information that the army had, that they wanted to provide to you, was obtained by you. How was it exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Of course I'll explain that. The information obtained by members of the corps, the 2nd Corps, were processed in their communications centre and converted from paper to computer. And after that, using a diskette, the file would be typed in. The contents of the information would be received on a diskette on our own computer. We would record that information under our own numbers, and we would add a sentence which would read, I think, "Taken over from the unit of the 2nd Corps," so that our superiors would be able to distinguish between the information we had obtained and the information obtained by that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, so it's perfectly clear, would the information that the army gave you be downloaded onto a disk and then given to the SDB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. My department would receive it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What they would receive would be the complete text of one or more intercepted communications that the army had obtained that particular day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. In one file, they could have one report, or five, or ten. It depended on how much material they would store in that file, how many reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could have the assistance of the usher, please, and I would like first of all shown to the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 302/2C. It's a four-page document in B/C/S. Witness W, if you just review that document before we place it on the ELMO, then we'll place it on the ELMO, and I want you to identify certain parts of that exhibit, please. For Your Honours' benefit, this particular exhibit has a four-page B/C/S text, and then the last conversation on the B/C/S of that particular document has been translated into French and English. So only one of the conversations on this 302/2C has been translated into French and English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, have you had a chance to review Prosecutor's Exhibit 302/2C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'm going to ask you -- Mr. Usher, if you would kindly place the top portion of the document so it is visible on the ELMO. Witness W, can you take a look at the document that's on the ELMO, and can you identify this document, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: As I have said, it is a document or information obtained by the PB of the 2nd Corps and forwarded to my department. My department would register that document under number 626 on the 14th of July, 1995, with an indication that it was taken over from the 2nd Corps. This was the standard practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date, "14/7/95", is the date that you received the communications that are contained in this document from the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. On that date, we received this file on a disk. We typed it into our computer on the edit programme that we used, and we added -- there's something I forgot to say. In the heading of such a document which would be forwarded to us by the corps, there would be their header with the contents. And instead of that, we would put our number, the date, and the indication that it was taken over from the 2nd Corps. Everything else is the same as the original text. It is the original text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The original text as received from the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you would turn to the last page of the B/C/S version. It has an ERN number of 00927783, and if you would place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, there appears on the ELMO now a conversation. Is this one of the conversations that you received from the army on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. That is within that one file that we received that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What Your Honours then have is a translation in French and English of that one conversation. I will read the translation into the record, and I would also direct Your Honours' attention to another exhibit which was tendered through Witness U. It is Exhibit 302/1A, 1B, and 1C. 1C is the handwritten version of this same conversation that was recorded by Witness U. Now, I will read into the record the translation of that last conversation that's found on Prosecutor's Exhibit 302/2C. "784700 MHz, Channel 3 at 2102 hours. Participants: Palma Duty Officer (Major Jokic) - Badem - X - Y. : Hello, Badem. Let me talk to Beara. B: Who wants to talk to him? : The Palma duty officer wants to talk to him. Beara is needed urgently, somebody needs him. The Superior Command urgently needs him, but he has to call me. B: Okay. P: Okay what? Give me Beara, don't hang up. J: Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the duty officer at Palma. I need Beara urgently. This is Major Jokic, who is that? Why the fuck are you not answering? Is Ostoja there? Is Brko there? Don't fuck around, the line has to be free and you must pick it up right away! Who is Ostoja? Is Ostoja there? Have him call me urgently. I will, I will. Hello! Hello! B: Here is Beara, you have him on the line. J: Hello! X: ... Hello. Is the operations duty officer looking for me? Go ahead. Vojanovic is not here, he's up at Snagovo. There are some problems there, at the line I've told you about. The Turks have pushed our guys back toward Crni Vrh. Y: ... X: Yes. I told him to consolidate the lines up there. That's it. J: Hello! B: Just a moment. One moment old man. J: Is that Beara? Jokic here. BE: ... J: We were together, Colonel, Sir. Number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently. BE: ... J: Number 155. That's, I mean, Superior Command, you go ahead and call them, you have, so I don't speak like this. BE: ... J: Yes. Hey. We have huge problems over here. BE: ... J: There are big problems. Well with the people, I mean, with the parcel. BE: ... J: Who? Drago is nowhere around. I don't know where the others are all day. BE: ... J: What? Call up there number 155 in the Superior Command and that's it. Okay, boss. BE: ... Why number 155? Where is that? J: Well, I can't tell you on this line, you know. You have it over there at signalsmen', who that is. BE: Yes? J: Bye. Remark: Thanks to the switchboard operator's mistake at Badem we recorded a conversation between X and Y, who couldn't be heard, while he was intercepting and the line 44 was open for Jokic." And that ends the translation of the last conversation that is found on Prosecutor's Exhibit 302/2C. Now, Witness W, I'd like to return to the work that was being performed by yourself and by members of your unit, and what I'd like you to do, please, is walk us through the procedures that were used by the SDB when they intercepted a communication. What I would like you to do is start with the time an individual who was attempting to intercept communications had a pair of headphones on and walk us through the procedure of recording that conversation and transmitting that conversation to your higher superiors.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we should go a step backwards first and then take a step forward. After looking at the frequency spectrum, searching it, and we were able to differentiate the frequency that was of interest to us and determine the exact channel we were interested in, and setting the radio devices so the operators could monitor that particular conversation and tape conversations of that kind in such a way that from the reception set, the receiving set, which was made up of several components, the NF signal or the voice signal would be brought onto the Uher tape recorder, and this recorded in volume audibly each conversation. As soon as a operator heard a conversation of this type going on, he would switch on the tape recorder, the tape recorder would then begin recording, and after having recorded the conversation, depending on its urgency, that is to say, if it was an urgent conversation, it would be -- that tape, that is to say, would be relayed to a free Uher and reproduced. Another operator, the second operator would replace the first operator and continue to monitor the conversation. Depending on the quality of the signal received, the conversation would then be reproduced directly into the computer, or if the signal was of a poorer quality, it would be reproduced onto a piece of paper. Very often, with the help of another colleague and a third colleague, perhaps, that is to say, I myself would do this work, if everything was audible, it would be recorded on the computer. If not, then parts of the conversation or words which were inaudible or we did not know what they meant or didn't hear them properly, we would place three dots. So if we didn't know several words, or even a paragraph, we would put asterisks in the middle so that the person reading would know that we had not been able to hear several words or even a whole paragraph, that it would be unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the conversation was audible, it would be recorded from the tape into the computer, and if there was a problem with the understandability or the quality of the transmission, then, from what I understand of your testimony, you would sit with colleagues, you would reduce the conversation on a piece of paper until there was some form of agreement as to its accuracy, and then it would be typed into the computer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those pieces of paper on which the conversation was recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, it was customary for pieces of paper of that kind to be set fire to. When we had a certain number of them, we would burn them. That was customary in our service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me then turn my attention to the procedure once again. Were the conversations that had been intercepted recorded in writing soon after or immediately after they had been received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: If they were very urgent, classed as very urgent information, then it was immediately processed. If it was not very urgent information, then it would also be processed in a short space of time afterwards, if nothing happened after that conversation; that is to say, if there were no other conversations, then that too would be processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if it wasn't an urgent conversation, how long after -- and I'm speaking in general terms -- how long after was it that it was reduced to writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Not long. It didn't wait long. Up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there an effort by your service to accurately record these conversations, in other words, make sure that each word that had been intercepted was accurately reproduced on the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It was essential that every word, literally every word be recorded and that it should be audible, properly heard. You couldn't guess because these were serious matters, and anything that was not sufficiently clear, not heard well enough, any word not heard well enough was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, how was it that you and your colleagues were able to identify the speakers in the intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have to say that we knew some of the speakers very well from the media, we knew their voices. Every citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and further afield were well acquainted with their voices. Many of them introduced themselves as well once the connection was established. So they would say, "Good morning. I'm so and so. I need so and so," and that would give us the information we needed about both participants, both parties. Very often there was a mediator in this communication; that is to say, the two parties would know each other but the intermediary would introduce them, so that was another way we learnt who the actors were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the situation where you could not identify the people who were speaking back and forth, how did you record that on your reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That too happened on several occasions, and we would use "X" and "Y" to denote those individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were the written records of the intercepted communications maintained by your agency in the regular course of business?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it was our duty to make up an archive, that was standard practice in our service, and to store the information we had arrived at, and that is what we did with these documents as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'm now going to put before you a number of exhibits, and I'd like to start with Prosecutor's Exhibit 303.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could have at your disposal Prosecutor's Exhibit 303 through Prosecutor's Exhibit 312. Mr. Usher, if you would first of all place the B/C/S version of Prosecutor's Exhibit 303 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'd like you to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 303, and let me ask you first of all, is this a document that was prepared by the SDB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document compiled by my department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that looking at this document? Use the pointer if need be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: In the heading it says "CSB/SDB," up here, "SDB Tuzla." Then you have the date and then there is a number for evidence which we keep in our archives today, and we have all these registration numbers down. Then there is a sentence which we always used as an introduction to all the conversations, and it was along the lines of this one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness W, at the bottom of this particular exhibit there appear to be a set of numbers, "JN160/JD065." What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to say, and that is perhaps the basic piece of information. As a signature, you have the names of people, the codes, the codes of the people who compiled the document. The first one, "JN160," denotes the man who recorded the conversation, taped the conversation, and the second code, that is to say, "JD065," is the man who reproduced the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I go into private session for just one or two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session, at least for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we're already in public session. Please continue, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, focusing on this particular communication, there are a number of initials that go down the left-hand side indicating the participants in the conversation. Am I correct that "K" stands for Krstic and "X" stands for Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read this communication into the record, starting at the upper left-hand corner: "CSB/Security Services Centre/-SDB/State Security Service/Tuzla Date: 12 July 1995 Number: 552 Very urgent On the above date, while monitoring the Zvornik-Vlasenica Radio Relay on frequency 785.000 MHz at 0735 hours, we recorded a conversation between someone called Krstic (K) and Lt. Colonel Krsmanovic (X). The conversation is as follows: K: Hello, is that Krsmanovic? X: Yes, go ahead. K: Listen! Write this down! X: Yes. K: Now, Pale, Visegrad, Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, Zvornik. Now, this, from all these places, 50 buses in total are to be at the stadium in Bratunac by 1700 hours. X: At 1700 hours at the Bratunac stadium. K: May very sure this is done. Is that clear? X: Understood. K: Go ahead. JN160/JD065."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have finished with this exhibit, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have just one remark to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I apologise. I think that in reading the frequency, you said "705", and the frequency was, in fact, "785".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I did make that mistake, thank you for the correction. That's correct. Mr. Usher, I would like to have 304C placed on the ELMO, with the date on the upper left-hand corner visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see that document, Witness W?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, is this a document that was prepared by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is also a document compiled by my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the B/C/S version there are two conversations, 557 -- number 557 and 558, and we have only translated 557, so the record is clear. I will read this into the record then, number 557, and I'm only reading that part of this B/C/S version that has been starting with 557. "A conversation between a certain Ognjenovic (O) and a General (G) from the Drina Corps Command in Vlasenica (code name Zlatar) took place on the same day, on the same frequency, on channel 5, at 0843 hours. The conversation proceeded as follows: G: Ognjenovic, what's happening around Jagnic (?). What have you heard? O: As far as I know, they heard here that the Turks are passing through a certain area and that they've found a path through the minefield. G: Okay, right. And has the commander ordered /them/ down in Konjevic Polje what's to be done? O: He ordered them, he ordered these guys down at Palma /code name/ (Zvornik Brigade) what to do and so forth. Both the MUP /Ministry of Interior/ and these guys ... G: Good, to the MUP in Konjevic Polje and Zvornik. Okay, bye." And at the bottom of the B/C/S version, there appears the letters "JN160/JD065".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness W, again the designation "JN160/JD065" is the same as what you previously described, is that correct, the person who heard the conversation and recorded it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at this document, can you tell us the date when this conversation was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. It is also the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next exhibit, Witness W. Mr. Usher, if you would kindly place 305 -- just one moment, please. Mr. Usher, if you would place 305B on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, will you take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 305B, and then I'll ask you some questions about it. Have you had a chance to take a look at that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an exhibit that was captured by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is the document captured by the members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: On the 12th of -- I think there's a mistake here, because it says "04/1995". I think that's a mistake, because 561, the number 561, it says the 12th of the 4th, "04". That's probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Number 561, we know, according to the order, what date was connected to that number. I apologise. What was it I said, the 12th of the 7th? That's probably a mistake. I didn't notice it until now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date do you believe this document was captured by members of your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have the exact date. I can check it out. I can check it, because I have a notebook, a diary, which records all the information that came in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you refer to your notebook, please, and confirm for us the date of this particular transmission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Therefore, it was like this: The date was -- just one moment, please. Let me find it. 561, 561. Just one moment, please. Yes. The 12th of July, 1995, I have it here, when the file was formed and when it was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness W. Now, I will read this document into the record, then. "CSB /Security Service Centre/-SDB /State Security Service/ Tuzla." "Date:", as recorded in the original document, "12 April 1995. Very urgent. Number: 561. On the aforementioned date while monitoring Pale Radio Relay, on frequency 785.000 MHz, Channel 5, at 1205 hours, we recorded a conversation between certain Ognjenovic (O) and General Krstic (K). The conversation was as follows: K: I said, are they passing over there? O: No, not near us. K: Then where are they? O: We are not sure. They passed down there and ran into a minefield in Duboki Potok, as you perhaps already know that. And how they came back, one group of 200 of them returned, but we don't know whether they passed or returned. K: Are there any remains of the dead in the place where they went through? O: Our guys didn't manage to get down there, since there are mines laid by our right neighbour. We don't have plans, so we didn't go down there. K: Collect the data as much as you can, call the units on the lines, particularly the ones on the right wing. Have them investigate everything, and then we'll get in touch. O: I don't know if you're going to be able to get in touch with Radika up there, so let me put you through. K: Go ahead and try. The conversation continues between Krstic and Krsmanovic (X). K: What happened with the buses? X: They should arrive in two minutes. K: Have them start immediately. X: Okay. We'll order them to move as soon as they arrive. K: Do you understand, to leave immediately. X: ... K: Go on. JN160/JD073."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Witness W, the "JN160/JD073" represents what you've told us previously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'll turn to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 306. Mr. Usher, if you would kindly place 306/C on the ELMO. Your Honours, there is a conversation that is 562 and a portion of 564 on the B/C/S. We have only translated the other conversation, 563, that's found on the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Witness W, can you identify this document as being a document that was prepared by members of your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is our document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what date was this document prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read this document into the record. I'm reading from 306/A: "CSB/Security Services Centre/-SDB/State Security Service/Tuzla Date: 12 July 1995 No. 563 On the aforementioned day while monitoring Zvornik-Vlasenica RR direction on frequency 785.000 MHz, Channel 11, at 12:20, we recorded a conversation between two unidentified men (X and Y). The conversation went as follows: X: What are we going to do about fuel? Y: I don't know. I told Miletic. X: Yes. Y: He doesn't know either. X: Those trucks are leaving from Ilijas, Pale, Visegrad, Zvornik, Sokolac, Rogatica. They are all coming here now. Y: Do you have any orders from up there? X: I have it from Krsto, where he ... ordered directly. That request went up there and I am thinking that it can't be 200 litres. It is 200 tonnes. And this morning I /or he/ left seven tonnes there for this equipment and two tonnes in Zvornik. That is nine. There is no more. Y: Call Mile. X: I'll call him right away." All right. We will now turn to the next document, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 307.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, again we'll follow the same procedure, if you would kindly put 307C, the B/C/S version, on the ELMO. Again, Your Honours, this is a document in the original B/C/S that has two identified conversations, number 570 and 571, and the attached translations only are to number 570.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, you've had an opportunity to take a look at this document. Can you first of all tell me, is this a document that was prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again. Is this a document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 307, is this a document that was prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is our document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date was this document prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: This document was also prepared on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read into the record this document. "Tuzla CSB/Security Services Centre/-SDB/State Security Service/ Date: 12 July 1995 Number: 570 On the above-mentioned day, intercepting the Zvornik-Vlasenica RR /radio-relay/ route on frequency 785.000, channel 5, we registered at 1250 hours a conversation between General Mladic (M) and an unidentified male person (X). The conversation proceeded as follows: X: Go ahead, General. M: Have these buses and trucks left? X: They have. M: When? X: Ten minutes ago. M: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to. X: I understand, General. M: Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the /?radio/ station. We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj. X: ... M: Indeed, let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road and remove the mines and obstacles ... leave the territory. X: Yes, General. JN160/JD073." Once again, Witness W, those numbers at the end stand for what you have previously testified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now turn to the next exhibit, which is 308.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, kindly put 308 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, is this a document that was prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that also is a document prepared by my service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say and I have said in the past, "is this a document prepared by your service," what I mean specifically by that question in respect of this document, the previous documents, and the documents to come, is this a document of an intercepted communication that was captured at the mountain top (redacted), where you were monitoring enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will read this document into the record. "Tuzla CSB/Security Services Centre/-SDB/State Security Service/ Date: 13 July 1995 Number: 597 On the above-mentioned day, intercepting at the Zvornik-Vlasenica RR /radio-relay/ route on frequency 785.000 MHz, channel 3, at 2035 hours, we registered a conversation between Major Obrenovic (O) and an unidentified General (G). The conversation proceeded as follows: O: General, sir, is that you? G: Yes. O: It's Major Obrenovic. G: Greetings. O: Listen, those ambushes I've been setting up over there on the wide road and on part of Glodansko Brdo - they just called me two minutes ago, there's a large column of Turks, three continuous kilometres long, from the school in Glodi. G: Wait! Listen, you can't talk like that on the phone. Call Mane, gather everybody and send them all up there right away. O: Mane's? G: Yes. O: Well, that's why I'm calling you. G: Tell them right away to gather and drive up there. As soon as possible. O: All right, understood. G: Come on chief, don't let anything through. O: We'll stop /them/. G: OK, take care. JN160/JD065." Once again, Witness W, do the number designations at the bottom of the page relate to what you have previously testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll now turn our attention to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 309.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, once again kindly place the B/C/S version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Examining the B/C/S version, Witness W, can you tell us whether this is a document of intercepted communications that were collected by your unit operating from the mountain top that you've previously identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that is our document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date was this particular communication intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The messages 605, 606, I can't see whether there are any others, were downloaded on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. President and Your Honours, we have only translated the conversation 606 in the B/C/S. On that same page there is conversation 605 and a portion of 607.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now read into the record number 606. Actually, Witness W, would you kindly read into the record the portion of the document that is before you in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you would have to move this down so the witness can see it. The portion under number 605, there's a small paragraph under 605, starting with the word "navedenog."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You're talking about conversation 605?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question. I had some confusion on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you return to 606, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will proceed in reading this into the record, then. "Number: 606 On the above-mentioned day, intercepting the Pale RR /radio-relay/ route on frequency 836.000, channel 13, we registered at 0805 hours a conversation between General Mladic (M) and an unidentified male person (X). The conversation proceeded as follows: M: Hello, friend. X: Good morning, brother. How are you? M: Fine, fine. You bet. X: A man can't get away from you in the newspapers, both foreign and local. M: I can't help it. (laughs) X: That's the way. Listen, I'll be brief and to the point: I was here just now with a narrow circle, you know, of friends here, and now it depends on you /as printed/. Are you going to be there these days? M: Well, I am after Sunday. X: But not today and tomorrow? M: I'm busy, but I am /here/ today if you can come over. X: You'll be there late in the afternoon? M: Until 1500 hours and then I'm going to the field. I'll be busy for two or three days and then I'm coming back. X: And where's Pepo? M: Pepo is in the field. The rest of the conversation was not interesting." I've concluded reading that particular document, and we'll now turn our attention to 310, Prosecutor's Exhibit 310.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, kindly place the B/C/S version of this document on the ELMO. This is a document, Your Honours, that has conversations numbered 605, 606, and 607 on the document, and we've only translated number 607.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the B/C/S document, Witness W, can you tell me if this was a document containing captured communications from the enemy that was prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, we prepared it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date did you prepare it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You would have to move it up so I can see the beginning. Yes, the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now read into the record the translation of the conversation number 607. "Number: 607 /handwritten:/ The pursuit On the same day, intercepting the Pale RR /radio-relay/ route on frequency 836.000 MHz, channel 5, at /?0810/ hours, we registered a conversation between two unidentified male persons (X and Y). The conversation proceeded as follows: X: Have a lot of their soldiers escaped to the woods? Y: Well, a lot did, the motherfuckers. X: You don't say. Y: Yeah, down there around Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. It's a real fuck-up now to chase them all out. X: Are they active or is it just mopping up that's going on? Y: Well, there's a little bit of everything. There are those who are mostly surrendering but some are still resisting. X: Uh-huh, it's not too dangerous? Y: Well, fuck it, this road here, from Zvornik towards us, is closed. It's not safe, they opened fire just yesterday at one of our Puchs /jeep/. X: Was there any damage? Y: No. A policeman was seriously wounded, but overall it's good. The road will stay closed until further notice. X: And have the colleagues arrived, the ones yesterday? Y: Radakovic said he's expecting them today. You mean these signalmen of ours? X: I meant the guy who went yesterday to Bijeljina. Y: Well, I don't know if he was able to get through. Radakovic told me that two captains and a staff sergeant are arriving today. But I don't know what happened because the road was closed. Just military vehicles, the 'special purposes' ones, can pass. X: So would you say that this area is sealed off? Y: Well, yes. X: They don't have anywhere to escape? Y: Well, that shouldn't happen. It's mostly under control, although it's woods out there ... X: In kilometres approximately, how many square kilometres is that? Y: I can't tell you now exactly. X: Is it basically five by five? Y: Yes, yes, something like that. They fucking know that terrain, they've spread out in the woods and it's very difficult. X: And do they have any food up there? Y: Hardly anything. X: They can sleep now wherever they want? Y: Well, they can't go on for long like that. They can for a short time, it's just that they can fuck us up somewhere. X: Yeah, they can. JN160/JD065." That ends my reading of this document. Again, Witness W, the numbers "JN160/JD065," does that represent what you previously testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, they mean the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll turn now, Witness W, to the next exhibit. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 311. Again, Mr. Usher, kindly place the B/C/S version of 311 on the ELMO. Your Honours, again this a document which contains multiple conversations in B/C/S. We have only translated the conversation numbered 610.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, is this a document that was prepared by your service, and does it contain the captured enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is also a conversation that we intercepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Could you show me, please? Yes. The 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will read this into the record. "Number 610. On the above date, while monitoring a Radio Relay Zvornik - Vlasenica on frequency 785.000 MHz, Ch. 3, at 0910 hours, we recorded a conversation between the Drina Corps Commander, Milenko Zivanovic (M) and Major Jokic (J). J: General, just to inform you, I just have some information about the Turks. M: What?
