J: They were crushed on Velja Glava and now there is a huge group moving towards the Drina, according to intelligence, towards Zljebac - Mladevac. The group is huge, absolutely enormous. M: How big is the group? J: It's huge. Ever since I heard this information I can't fucking believe it. M: Who told you that? J: Thousands of 'em. Our intelligence officer sent us an info. M: Which intelligence officer? J: Dusko Vukotic. M: Where are you calling from now? J: From here, as a duty officer. M: And where are they headed? J: According to our intelligence organs they spread out from Velja Glava, they think in this direction, so now they're going back towards Mladevac and towards Zljepce over there to Novo Selo, you know? M: Yes, yes, Mladevac. Good. Good. I know that. J: Yes, Kula Grad, to the left of Kula Grad. M: Mane needs to be informed immediately. (Mane, a MUP employee, most likely a chief). J: Whom should I inform? M: The Zvornik Public Security Centre. They're there now. The army is doing other work at the moment. J: The Chief of Staff, Obrenovic, is coming now so we'll take steps immediately. M: Mane should finish that off for you because Mane has policemen in Konjevic Polje and Zvornik, and we are not talking about such a large number of people, they're lying. J: Is that so? M: Take care. JD073/JD065." May I have just a moment, Mr. President. My colleague has passed me a note. My colleague has brought to my attention there appears to be two sentences that have not been translated on to the English version of 610, and on the B/C/S version, 311/B, it appears that the first two sentences at the bottom of that page have not been translated at least on to the English version. I think I can read the first sentence in B/C/S. It appears to say: "Hello, Major Jokic." The second sentence I cannot read, but we will go back to the Language Service Section with this particular exhibit and submit a more complete and revised version of this. Witness W, now let me turn to the last exhibit in this series. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 312. Mr. Usher, if you would show this to the witness, because the reproduction, at least my reproduction, is not very clear. Let him inspect it first, and then it can be placed on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, please place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, is this a document of a recorded intercepted communication that was captured by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this captured -- strike that. On what day was this communication captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I can't see it very well on this copy. I can't even see the number quite well, whether it is "664". If it is, I could check in my diary regarding the date. But most probably it is the 16th of July, 1995, as far as can be discerned from this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- may I have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I'm going to see if I can get a better copy of this. I'll ask you a question after the break. We'll try to get a better copy of this. In the meantime, we'll reserve that question, and let me pursue this. Looking at this document, are you able to see whether this was a document that was, in fact, prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it is obviously a document prepared by my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, since the witness has not identified the document number or the date, I'm reluctant to read in the translation. So if we could have a break, at which point I will endeavour to get a better copy for the witness, so then I can proceed. This is my last document, by the way, and then I will conclude my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Harmon. We were waiting for the end of the presentation of these documents, but we understand. So we're going to have a break, a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. We have resolved the issue. I have a better photocopy of the exhibit I had intended to show the witness earlier; it is 312/C bis. If you could show that, Mr. Usher, first to the witness so he can identify the date and the number of the intercepted communication, we'll place that on the ELMO and proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I apologise for presenting to you earlier a poor reproduction of this exhibit, but now that you've had an opportunity to examine it, let me ask you first of all, is this a communication that was intercepted by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. That is the text of the message that my unit registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day was this particular message intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will read this translation of 312/C bis into the record. "CSB/Security Services Centre/-SDB/State Security Service/Tuzla Date: 16 July 1995 Very urgent No: 664 On the above date, monitoring the Pale Radio Relay on frequency 836.000 MHz, Channel 13, at 1615 hrs, we recorded a conversation between Main Staff Duty Officer and General Mladic, who was inaudible. The conversation was as follows: : Good day General, Sir. : Well, it's like this. I've just sent a telegramme to Toso. Well, the President called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic had arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory. Since I have no communication with him, I asked the duty officer to urgently connect me with him: to /?have him/ send me a telegram with that information and not to do anything without authorisation until he receives our answer. Now I'm waiting for them to call me because Pandurevic hasn't called for the last four ... : Yes, of course. No, but there are both fighters and civilians. : Nobody is playing around, that's just the information we got. I spoke to Krsto down there. He says it's going well but I ... he didn't say how far they got, but he says it's going well. : According to Maric, yes ... is solved. : This morning, last night, they captured equipment at four UN check points, down in Zepa, took them to the base, confiscated the equipment. : Good, there were no other major problems, up on Majevica there was something but that has been resolved. : Bye. JD073/JD065." Witness W, I have just a couple of questions about this particular conversation. The first is: This conversation is only a one-sided conversation that you were able to intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. We just heard one of the speakers, and we wrote it down that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The numbers that appear at the end of this document, "JD073/JD065," are those code numbers for members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've concluded with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to return very briefly to Prosecutor's Exhibit 306, which, in the form it was presented to Your Honours this morning, omitted the second page. So I have had a new document prepared; it is Exhibit 306/C bis. Mr. Usher, if you would put the last page of that document on the ELMO, and particularly what I would like to have on the ELMO, Mr. Usher, are the numbers that appear at the bottom of the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, at the bottom of this now-complete document -- you've earlier testified about it -- do there appear to be two sets of numbers on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this document that is now complete, do the numbers "JN160/JD073" appear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they do appear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, consistent with your previous testimony, indicates the identity of persons involved with this particular communication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With that, Mr. President and Your Honours, I've concluded my direct examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic. Witness W, you're now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Petrusic. Please go ahead. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let me say good afternoon to you, Witness W.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In performing your duties, you worked in the same building where the members of the army were located, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, for anti-electronic warfare and reconnaissance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you proceed according to the same rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I don't know which rules you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any written rules or regulations which you, that is to say, your service, were duty-bound to abide by in the performance of your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, apart from the housekeeping rules of conduct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether rules of that kind existed in units -- in the units of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I think that it is clear to you that I am a member of the SDB, and I don't know what rules they used or whether they had any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, or the service to which you belonged, in that location keep a diary of any kind, of daily orders or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We were not a military organisation. That is typical of a military organisation. It is typical for the service to which I belong that all the papers on which the messages are recorded, after use, after they've been sent on, be destroyed, especially as we were located in premises not owned by us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the service that you belonged to, did you have a work plan of any kind from that service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Nothing specific in concrete terms. At the beginning, I described what we did and what our basic tasks were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. We're having difficulty following him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many sets of equipment for interception did your service dispose of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. We had three sets of equipment. However, we also had some other receivers which were able, without a complete set, to receive certain waves and frequencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: What was interesting for us, of course, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your service --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. There appears on the transcript -- excuse me, Mr. Petrusic. There appears on the transcript "[No interpretation]" for one of your questions, which makes the record incomplete.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter wasn't able to hear. There was something wrong with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon, thank you very much. It is page 90, line 22. You have the answer, but no question. The question has not been recorded in the LiveNote. [Page 80].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Were the frequencies memorised," was the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Do I need to answer that question again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. The frequencies were memorised, those that we found interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, the Prosecutor asked you in detail about the procedure of reception of messages, their transcription. But what the Defence is interested in, is the reception of that message and what happened to it after that or, rather, how it was typed into the computer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: As I have already recounted, the way in which a message was received, recorded, and reproduced. It is processed in the computer, encrypted, and then forwarded to the base; that is, to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it forwarded to headquarters by means of computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Excuse me. What do you mean when you say "by computer methods"? It was processed in the computer and forwarded with the help of a modem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was forwarded by fax modem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to talk about the way in which messages were transmitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't insist on that, but was that method, the one you do not wish to talk about, used from the 12th of July onwards during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were supplied with this computer equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Another department I headed in 1992 already had a computer, so the computer in this facility was not available from the beginning, but I received it. I couldn't tell you the exact date, but that can be established on the basis of the encrypted files, because in the period when I didn't have a computer of my own, the information was forwarded through the communications system of the 2nd Corps, to the command of the 2nd Corps, and then from the 2nd Corps Command, information was forwarded to the headquarters of my service on a disk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When one of your messages was forwarded in the method you have described, do you know whether there was a reception stamp on that message, a stamp confirming receipt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I don't understand what kind of stamps you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you forwarded a message to your superior service, did it register somewhere that it had received that message?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You see, that also enters into the question of the method of transmission of information, but everyone knows that information has to be registered upon reception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had some sort of confirmation that the information had been received.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the Uher tape recorder tapes, you have recorded tapes. What happened to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I think your question was not phrased properly. The Uher tapes did not contain cassettes but conversations, taped conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. So you tape a cassette, that is, you tape conversations on a cassette. What happens to that cassette?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It depends on the type of conversation, its importance, and other characteristics which would determine how it would be kept, if at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they are the conversations that we heard read out today and which were read by the Prosecutor and which you confirmed, have those conversations been preserved on tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I could not answer that question. I think that it is a sensitive question and I do not wish to answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it because you don't know or because you don't want to answer it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have already said what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we could go into a private session and Your Honours could explore this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are going into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we are in public session, so you may continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 303/C of the Prosecution which you confirmed -- and it is a conversation between Krsmanovic and a certain Krstic -- on which grounds do you identify that certain Krstic if he did not introduce himself, nor did the other participant in the conversation call him by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: An excellent question. You see yourself that this is not the very beginning of the conversation, and usually what happens is, in that few seconds until the button is released of the pause, one, two, or three words are uttered, and obviously those words were spoken. Otherwise, certainly the words "a certain Krstic" would not be there. Another matter, and I shall assist you again, is that in this period of time we were not focusing on this channel intensively because we knew that this channel was covered by the army. So when we had nothing else to do, we too would monitor this channel, together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, you mean that this frequency, 785, that this frequency was covered both by you and the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, in those pauses that we had on our frequencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, reviewing these conversations that were shown to you today, I note that they mostly refer to this frequency of 785.000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: What do you want of me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you didn't use it frequently, but the conversations shown to you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They are very few in number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you agree with me, then, that the conversations shown to you in the course of the day were captured from the frequency 785.000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Of course. I confirmed that several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, it seems to me that you still have in front of you Exhibit 303/C. In the header, after the date and the number, there is the sentence: "On the above date, while monitoring the Radio Relay Zvornik-Vlasenica on frequency 785.000 ..." et cetera, you recorded a conversation between these two participants. My question is: If one of the participants was outside the Zvornik-Vlasenica direction, can you intercept him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You mean if one of the parties is calling from Pale, for instance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one of the participants is outside the radio relay Zvornik-Vlasenica, can you record that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Technically speaking, and that is the only way I can view things, I receive the signal on that segment of the route, conditionally speaking. So everything I register on that direction and I consider to be interesting, I take it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, when you're talking about the direction, you are talking about the radio relay direction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the evidence shown to you or, rather, the conversations shown to you mainly relate to the Zvornik-Vlasenica radio relay. So there are two destinations or, rather, two locations. In Exhibit 305/B, you begin your report with the same sentence: "On the above-mentioned date, while monitoring Pale Radio Relay ..." without the other location of the radio relay direction being indicated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You've obviously found a mistake in the written report, an error, and I should like to clarify something. On a radio relay route, we can hear the complete telephone communication taking place along that route regardless of where the participants may be at that particular moment. What does that mean? It means that a participant in the communication may be from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say this is an error?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you just mentioned the radio relay route Pale, without indicating the other location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to explain things, that frequency is not linked to locations. A frequency is the route that we intercepted, and along that route, at the intercepted wavelengths, we captured conversations which may have been spoken in Rogatica or Bijeljina, and as far as I can remember there was some conversations coming from Serbia all along that one and the same route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this case, as you said, that was an error.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Of course. This is an error on the part of the person who was typing this report. Frequency 785 determines the route that was intercepted. Pale, Zvornik, Vlasenica, et cetera, those are not determinant. So in this specific case, "Pale" is the error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't me who said it was an error, you said it was an error and I repeated it. But, sir, we're talking about one and the same frequency here, both when we're talking about the Pale route and the Zvornik-Vlasenica route, and that is 785.000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I'm afraid you don't understand me. I am claiming or, rather, noting and stating that in Exhibit 305/B the word "Pale" has been erroneously written, because it should be "the Radio Relay Route Zvornik-Vlasenica." That is how we called it. So here a substitution was made. It is the frequency that determines the direction at that particular moment in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about Exhibit 305, where you identify General Krstic as a participant in the conversation, whom again the other participant does not identify in the course of the conversation, was the same method of identification used that you described with respect to Exhibit 303/C, and that conversation was one between Krsmanovic and Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Some were -- halfway through the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, I explained the way in which we recognised voices. Maybe 1073, the operator, recognised the participant by his voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these two exhibits, 305/B and 303/C, we have the same person listening in, intercepting the conversation. In 303/C, he describes him as a certain Krstic, and 305/B, as General Krstic. So it is the same operator and I think it is the same date, the 12th of July. There is a few hours' difference between 7.35 and 12.05 when the second conversation was intercepted. Can you tell us, if the message was intercepted by the same person, is it possible that in one case he describes him as "a certain" and in the second case as a specific person, that is, as "General Krstic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Something that you should know is that in these two conversations, there's 1065 and 1073, two different reproducers; that's one point. The second point, the person who is recording and the person who is reproducing are physically in the same room, so even if that did happen so quickly, it explains why there was no dilemma in the second conversation. There are several methods, as I have explained, for the recognition of voices, and I don't think I should repeat them. I have also explained that there are sound recordings which do not start from the very beginning. The first sentence was spoken, for instance: "This is General Krstic. Give me so and so." That first sentence is not recorded, and there are such recordings with that first sentence missing, if you're following me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Exhibit 308/C --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to leave the exhibits for the time being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- by hand we see in the upper right-hand corner, as far as I was able to decipher it, it says "Search for civilians -- pursuit of civilians." Could you tell us whether you know who wrote that down, on what occasion, why and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Personally, I believe that that has absolutely nothing to do with the reproduction of conversations, and I would rather not comment on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same words can be found on Document 310/C.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: My answer is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I apologise. On Document 310/C, in the middle -- at the top of the page, it says "pursuit" again. No, it says "capture of civilians," I'm sorry, at the top of the page. And in the middle of the page, it says "pursuit" in handwriting. My question is: is that your handwriting? Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have given my answer. I think that that has absolutely nothing to do with reproduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Document 309/C -- so with reference to this document, 309/C, your answer is the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have no reason to change my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, sir, whether this photocopy of these documents -- are they true to the original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the original documents themselves, are these words written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have one more document that I'd like to show with the same contents. This is 311/B. I assume that your answer is the same. Is it? For purposes of the transcript, in the right-hand side of the page, towards the end of the page, it says "pursuit".

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has not answered the question. I am waiting for an answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I understood you, you just noted that in the right-hand corner it says the word "pursuit". You didn't ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you wrote that or someone else in your service subordinate to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I have already stated my answer and do not consider that that influences the quality or the aspect of the conversation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, let me start with Exhibit 303. You were asked by my colleague Mr. Petrusic a question about how it is that you could identify someone called Krstic in this conversation when the name "Krstic" is not mentioned anywhere in the text. And as I understood your answer, and I would appreciate your clarifying this for me, when the conversation was being intercepted, initially the tape recorder that captured the conversation was not on, and between the point in time when the conversation was first heard by the intercept operator and the time it took to depress the tape recorder, a certain portion of the conversation was omitted from the tape. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you understand that correctly. That did happen on occasion, and I warned of that in a portion of my testimony. I said that these were very serious matters and that in all cases, when we were not absolutely sure who we were dealing with, we would always place the letter "X" or "Y" to denote that individual. Similarly, if we were not 100 per cent certain of a letter, we would place a question mark next to the name. I hope that from reading all these documents, that you have been able to realise that all we did was serious work and that it was profound work as well. Thank you. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stay with this particular document, and let me put myself in the shoes of the person who is monitoring the conversation, who hears the conversation. Let me ask you for your observations on this conversation. Is this a long conversation, if you can tell from just looking at the text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The conversation was not long. Therefore, the conversation is short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With an intercept operator who hears a conversation and knows that he is a little late in capturing all the conversation, in other words, is a little late in depressing the button, what steps, if any, are taken to record or identify the speakers in the initial omitted sentence of the conversation? Were any steps taken at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put it this way: The operator, when the conversation starts, can lose a split second of time, and when he releases the stop button, in releasing the stop button he has already heard the participants. However, and straightaway at that very same moment he records the participants, whether we know who they are or not; that is to say, whether they have introduced themselves or not, whether they are known or not known to the operator. At that very same moment, we record the time the conversation starts. At the same time, we also record the numbers on the tape recorder so that we can go back and reproduce the conversation from the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, generally speaking, when an operator hears a conversation and a party is identified, the first step, I take it, is to depress the button on the tape recorder, and the second step is to attempt to record the missing portions or the identities of the speakers, if that's possible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That's correct. That is precisely the order. We record the identity of the party, if we know who that is or whether this was stated, so we record the time of the conversation, the numbers from the meter, and afterwards we record the frequency, the channel on which the conversation took place. Of course, all this is linked up to the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me change the topic. My colleague asked you a series of questions about the Zvornik-Vlasenica radio frequency, 785 megahertz, and if I could have the witness shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 139. Mr. Usher, if you could place on the ELMO the lower left quarter of this document. If you would raise it just a little more, please. Raise it up, please, Mr. Usher. That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you seen this document before coming to court, Witness W?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the communications route that used 785.000 megahertz on this document, and could you point it out to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I think that's the route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, do you see a line that goes from the location Panorama and goes up towards Zlatar, and there are some numbers midway between those two locations specifically saying "785.000 megahertz"? If you would move your pointer up. No, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I approach the witness and just point on the exhibit to what I'm referring to. For the record, Mr. President and Your Honours, I've indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 139 the numbers "785.000 megahertz" midway between the Zlatar notation and the Panorama location, the Panorama location being the centre of the radiating lines going out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, can you -- what does this "785.000 megahertz" that I've pointed out to you indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The frequency 785, it is 785 megahertz, and it denotes the frequency of the route or the bearer of the signal who, within his composition, has 24 channels, if you can understand that. It is the upper and lower sound volume which has 24 sound-speaking channels. Now, what does that mean? It means that each of these frequencies can bear a load of 24 telephone conversations in one direction. That means in one direction, a conversation in one direction, unilateral, one-way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, I want to understand radios, I can assure you, better than I know them now, but I'm learning every day. Let me ask you this: When there are two speakers in a radio communication, the first speaker is physically located at Location A and the second speaker who is receiving the conversation is located at Location B. When a radio communication is transmitted from Point A to Point B, does it have to go through a relay centre on some occasions or can it be transmitted directly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It depends on where the two parties in the conversation are located. There are relay centres which direct the direction, and the two parties in a conversation -- I explained this a moment ago -- need not be in Zlatar or Panorama for the conversation to be heard. So they can be in another location linked to that portion through which the signal must pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you a concrete example, Witness W. Could one party to the conversation, for example -- strike that. The conversation that you intercepted that is the subject of Prosecutor's Exhibit 303A was intercepted along a certain frequency, the Zvornik - Vlasenica Radio Relay. Now, the frequency is identified as 785.000. Based on that information in this report, can you point on this map to tell me the approximate route or the area where this conversation was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I claim that the conversation passed Route 785, passed through it. That is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you the next question, which is: Could one of these speakers in this conversation have been physically located -- and for the sake of example -- at Bratunac, which is on the right side of the map at Badem? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, therefore, when the conversation was being communicated to a location, for example, at Zlatar or at Vlasenica, the conversation, as I understand it, would pass from Bratunac, through the communications centre which is at Panorama, and then be repeated up the line to Vlasenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, therefore, when you intercepted the communication, it was intercepted somewhere along the line in the direction going -- I'm sorry, at this megahertz, 785.000 megahertz, and it was intercepted at that particular frequency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to conclude, the physical location of the persons at either end of the communication -- I'm sorry, at the transmitting end of the communication isn't necessarily Panorama, which is the centre of the radiating lines in this diagram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness W. I have just one question, and I would like to ask you this question knowing that it's not a professional question. I'm a layman; I'm not scientifically involved like you. You said that there are some sound recordings not starting from the beginning, and certain recordings would have the first sentence missing. You mentioned as an example, saying, "This is General Krstic. Give me so and so." Then you said later that when you don't capture the beginning, you record first and then you start to find the identity of the party. When you missed the first part and you record, then later you try to record the identity of the party. How do you find the identity of the party if it was not captured at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the beginning of the conversation, he might have identified himself. He could have stated his name; he could have done that even before the operator switched the tape recorder on, but the operator heard it and recorded it on paper. So the two parties -- and the two parties can, of course, identify themselves in the course of the conversation. However, there is another thing. Very often the voices can be recognised. In the course of one day you have the same person having several conversations, and of course the operator can remember the sound of his voice. Or another case, he might say that he is the corps commander, for example, and we did have a corps commander at the time so we would know who that person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In fact, this leads me to a more specific question, because you said textually there are several methods for the recognition voices. I'm speaking of scientific methods, the way you can have a voiceprint or that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If we apply this to Prosecution Exhibit 303/A, when you say the conversation was between someone called Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, according to your knowledge, how did they detect that it was Krstic? Because it's announced as a fact. He said it was as if he knew it but it did not come in the conversation. In the conversation they said, "Hello, is that Krsmanovic?" but the other doesn't say, "Hello, is that Krstic?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to explain that in the way I did. Quite certainly the operator who did this did not do it -- did not record something that he imagined. It either happened or what might have happened was that the time needed for the operator to switch on the tape recorder, the words "Krsmanovic here" -- I beg your pardon, "Krstic here" might already have been spoken, or he recognised his voice. But at all events I maintain that we always aspired to have the names of people quite certain and sure because of everything that followed; that is to say, the people who worked professionally in these matters, in my own service, do not any erroneous data or information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it becomes a matter of practice that they always know who is speaking, and then they just mention it without having to prove it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Any dilemma that might exist would be recorded as well. So if he wasn't certain, then there would be an "X," or if it wasn't audible enough, if he didn't hear just one letter of the name, once again you would have a question mark next to the name, which means that it associates that name but it need not be, because one letter might change a name. So unless you have heard a name completely, we would put "X" or "Y."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's quite satisfactory. Thank you. Just as a hypothetical question. In the conversation in the same document, there was an order by, what you called, someone called Krstic asking for 50 buses in total at the stadium in Bratunac, by 1700 hours. Could there be any possibility of knowing if he's calling from Bratunac, for instance, or this was completely impossible for those who are recording? Was he speaking from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We were not able to locate this with any precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or approximately, you cannot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We only knew that the conversation passed by that segment, and we intercepted it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, two of these intercepts do identify in the paper form General Krstic as being a participant in the conversation, 303 and 305, and then there are several intercepts which you or whoever prepared them doesn't identify. It says, "Unidentified General" or "Unidentified X" or "Y" and you had told us that very often the person listening can sometimes identify because they recognise the voice, as well as a formal introduction that goes on the tape. My question is: Since all of these intercepts that we've been dealing with over the last hour all took place over a couple of days, July 12th to July 14th, would it be reasonable to infer, since General Krstic, by whatever means was identified as the participant in two of them, that that pretty much means that he would not have engaged in any of the intercepts where the people are unidentified, like "Unidentified General," or else his voice would have been recognised, or is that not a fair inference to draw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I hope that I have understood you correctly now, and you must try and understand me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I forgot to mention a detail which can bring the operator into a dilemma, that is to say, that he cannot say the name, that is, the quality of the connection, the quality of the sound. Perhaps it was an individual who took part in the previous conversation, but because of the quality of the communication connection itself -- what I want to say is that we didn't want to send out any disinformation to our head office ourselves; that was not our intention at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you are saying that you erred on the side of being very conservative, and even if you thought somebody might be the same person, you wouldn't put it down unless you had something more certain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is precisely right. We would have to be 100 per cent certain in order to write somebody's name down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Of course we didn't know that there would be The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness W, you have just asserted something that I was going to ask you, because you said that you were doing serious work but that at the time - then - you didn't know that you would be working for the Tribunal as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I did not. Not in my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You saw a series of documents produced by your service, if I can put it that way. Do you know who underlined those documents, did the underlining?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, this is my answer: I think that it was a type of working document that you have been handed; the working documents. So why should I speak on that subject if it was the task of my service? I think that is sufficient, to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question. If the document 557 -- so we have document 557, and the date is the 12th of July. Document 563 has the same date, that is to say, the 12th of July, and another document, 563 -- no, document 561, what date should it have? Have you got a pencil and could write it down, a piece of paper -- Mr. Usher, please -- because it's more visible that way. So document 561, dated the 12th of April -- I beg your pardon. No, I jumped the gun. Let me start again. Document 557, 12th of July; 563, 12th of July. What is the date that document 561 should have? Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It would be logical that the same date would be on that document too; that is logical. However, there is the possibility of the fact that it was sent -- that is to say, I'm not quite certain of which document we mean, whether it was a document taken over, but it might have been processed during the night and entered in the following day, or that it was somewhere between day and night. I would have to see. I would have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is sufficient. In fact, it was a question put to you by the Prosecutor. It was a date which, in your opinion, was in error. But it could happen through logical deduction, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question for you. I'm not sure that I understood something properly. What is the date when you began working in that building with the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: There is an exact date. I know that it was in December 1994 when the first report was sent out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. We can see that the 12th of July, there was a lot of work on the 12th of July for you. We can also see that the operator JN160 worked throughout the day of the 12th, more or less, because the documents have that date, and also on the 13th and 14th. Let us take the 12th for a moment. If that particular individual listened in once and recognised the voice of General Krstic, is it logical to suppose that he could recognise it in all the intercepts, subsequent intercepts, except the ones where you said there was a poor communication line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It is not logical to recognise it every time. Let me try and explain why. Nobody could take on the responsibility of saying, "I heard the voice once and I'll be able to recognise it every subsequent time." First of all, this is because we didn't only listen to Krstic. Had we only listened to Krstic and had we only had Krstic, then that could probably be possible, the operator in case could say that that was the case. But you always had to have elements which would determine identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: During those same days, on the other side in your service I think you said that there were at least two people working there, the operator, that is to say, Operator JN160, and the other person, Operator JD073. How did you work together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Quite simple. We had a room the size -- that is to say, it was three and a half metres by three metres in size. And I've already said that we had a bed there and the device and a table, and that was enough. We were there all the time. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my other question: The documents that we have seen have to do with two frequencies largely, 785 and 836. Let's leave out the other numbers. We see that the 785 frequency produced at least -- that is to say, the documents were obtained on channels 5, 11 and 3. The other one, let us leave behind for the moment. Now, these channels, 5, 11 and 3, were they part of the 24 possible channels on the same frequency or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Very often -- that is to say, I have not mentioned this so far. In identifying the individual channels within the frameworks of those 24 channels, we knew exactly who was using which, but with the proviso that from that telephone, somebody else could call from that telephone. So we never dared say exactly who it was. It was a telephone in his office, for example, but the courier could have used it, the secretary could have used it, a soldier could have used it, and so on and so forth. So we knew 100 per cent that on that route, the telephone belonged to so and so. That's what we could say for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the same person monitor the same channel or could the same person switch to other channels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We had distinct channels, and as we didn't have many personnel, only (redacted), we mostly used those few channels or listened to those few channels and frequencies and all the things that we have said; identified the channel, who it belongs to, et cetera, et cetera. So it wasn't one person who was associated to one channel exclusively, because we didn't have sufficient people. But we also did not cover hundreds of frequencies at the same time. That was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So thank you very much. We have learned a lot about radio today, and so we wish to thank you for teaching us and, above all, for speaking seriously. Thank you for your testimony. I think we have some exhibits to admit, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have shown and introduced through this witness's testimony and laid the foundation for a number of exhibits. These are exhibits which were not contained in the notebooks but which are distinct pieces of paper, and I can identify them. And I would move for their admission, obviously understanding the Court's previous ruling. But this constitutes a distinct set of documents, and I will identify them. 303A, B and C; 304A, B and C; 305A, B and C; 306A, B and C and C bis; 307A, B and C; 308A, B and C; 309A, B and C; 310A, B and C; 311A and B; 312A, B and C and C bis. We would tender those documents into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. But in view of the ruling of the Chamber, perhaps they should be put in the same package, and I think that is what Mr. Petrusic is about to ask. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Petrusic, you see that the Prosecutor has facilitated your task a little, so please try and facilitate the task of the Prosecution as well. So review all the documents so as to be able to take a position as soon as possible, please. I think we have come to the end of your testimony, Witness W. We thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you success in your work and a safe journey to your country. We will now adjourn. We will be here again tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
